p: Bir Hakeim was a fortress built by the Ottomans at the crossing of two Bedouin paths. It stood at the southern end of the Gazala line, a series of brigade-sized defensive boxes that the British Eighth Army held west of Tobruk. On 14 February 1942 the 1st Free French Brigade took over the box, which was surrounded by 50,000 mines. The brigade had a fighting strength of 3,000 men, with the 13th Demi-Brigade of the Foreign Legion as its backbone, and by mid-May it had dug 1,200 entrenchments, foxholes and gun emplacements. The Axis plan sent the armour around the box while the Italian 132nd Armoured Division Ariete neutralised it.

On the morning of 27 May an Italian tank battalion of the Ariete Division, with 60 tanks, charged the minefield and wire. It lost 31 tanks and a self-propelled gun, and ten tanks that got through were knocked out by 75 mm anti-tank guns. From 2 June the position was shelled and bombed, and Stuka dive-bombers raided it more than twenty times, but the well-built positions were almost invulnerable. On 6 June the 90th Light Division attacked with pioneers, who cleared passages through the minefields.

From 8 June Rommel directed attacks from the north with part of the 15th Panzer Division, and the perimeter was forced back. On 10 June, with ammunition almost gone, the fort took the largest air raid of the siege, by 100 Stukas. After dark sappers cleared a narrow passage through the mines on the western face. Kœnig left at the head of the column in a car driven by Susan Travers, an Englishwoman serving with the Foreign Legion, and most of the brigade broke through troops of the 90th Light Division to reach lorries and ambulances sent by the British 7th Motor Brigade.

Thomas Buell and Ken Ford give the French losses as 141 dead, 229 wounded and 814 taken prisoner, with 53 guns and 50 vehicles; the Axis lost 3,300 dead or wounded and 227 captured, with 164 vehicles destroyed and 49 aircraft shot down. The defence had lengthened the Axis supply route around the Gazala line and gave the British time to recover from their defeat in the Cauldron, and the delay influenced the cancellation of Operation Herkules, the Axis invasion of Malta. Tobruk still fell ten days later. Both sides used the battle for propaganda, and Winston Churchill declared the Free French to be the Fighting French.

notes: I read the siege section in excerpts (long lines were cut off in my view), so the number of men who got out, given at the end of the 'Retreat' section, is not stated.
Porch (2004) gives 845 prisoners against Buell and Ford's 814; I gave the latter with its authors.

Left out for room: Douglas Porch's report that Hitler ordered captured German political refugees to be killed, an order Rommel ignored; and the supply convoys that reached the fort (fifty trucks on 31 May).
The article has the 3rd Indian Motor Brigade overrun on 27 May with about 440 men lost; left out as outside the fort.
